items.paragraph: Many customs presented as ancient turn out, on inspection, to be quite recent: a ceremony said to go back centuries may have been devised a few generations ago, often at a moment when a group felt its identity threatened. Debunkers enjoy pointing this out, as if exposing the recent origin of a tradition exposed it as a fraud. The inference is too quick. A tradition does not need to be old to do what traditions do, which is to bind people to one another and to a shared past, and a recent invention that people adopt wholeheartedly is no less real in its effects than one inherited unbroken. What the discovery should change is not our regard for the practice but our belief about its history; the claim to antiquity may be false while the attachment it supports is genuine.

items.paragraph: Moral rules such as 'do not lie' or 'keep your promises' are often attacked by pointing to exceptions: surely one may lie to save a life, or break a trivial promise to help someone in danger. items.paragraph: A measurement can be precise without being accurate. If a scale consistently reads two kilograms too heavy, repeated weighings of the same object will agree closely with one another, and that agreement may inspire confidence, yet every reading is wrong by the same amount. Precision describes how tightly repeated results cluster; accuracy describes how close they lie to the true value. The distinction matters because the usual way of checking a result, repeating it, reveals only the first. A systematic error survives any number of repetitions untouched, and can be exposed only by comparing the instrument with an independent standard or a different method. Consistency is therefore reassuring about random noise but silent about bias.

items.paragraph: The undo command looks like a minor convenience, but it changes how people use software. When every action can be reversed, users explore: they try an unfamiliar menu, apply a filter just to see what it does, delete a paragraph to judge whether the essay reads better without it. Where actions are permanent, the same users grow cautious, read instructions first and stick to the few operations they already trust. Undo, in other words, lowers the cost of a mistake, and when mistakes are cheap, experimenting becomes rational. Much of what people learn about a program they learn by just such trial and error, so a design that forgives errors also turns out to be one that teaches.

items.paragraph: It is often said that a gift made anonymously is morally superior to one made publicly, since the anonymous donor cannot be seeking praise and so must be acting from pure generosity. Recording a usage is not endorsing it. Readers who want advice on what is appropriate in formal writing are entitled to it, and usage notes and style guides exist to provide it. The mistake lies in expecting one book to do both jobs and then blaming it for doing the one it set out to do.

options.C: Cannon made castles obsolete, and the costly fortresses replacing them were affordable only to rulers taxing whole realms, so defence costs moved power from lords to the centre.

items.paragraph: When cannon became powerful enough to batter down tall stone walls, the castle of a local lord lost much of its value as a refuge. The answer was a new kind of fortification: low, thick ramparts with angled bastions that deflected shot and allowed defenders to cover every approach. Such works were enormously expensive to build and to garrison, far beyond the means of most nobles, and so the ability to hold territory passed increasingly to rulers who could raise taxes across a whole realm. A change in military technology thus did political work, strengthening central authority at the expense of local power, not by any decision to centralise but through the rising cost of defence.

options.A: Schools should abolish grouping by birth year and adopt mixed-age classes everywhere, since every teacher knows that children of one age differ in readiness.
options.B: Older pupils in a mixed-age class gain more than younger ones, since explaining material to others is the surest way of consolidating one's own understanding of it.
options.C: Sorting pupils by age rests on a convenient but false premise; mixed-age classes bring real benefits, and their demands call for trained teachers rather than rejection.
options.D: Mixed-age teaching usually fails because teachers cannot manage several levels at once, which is why schools still sort their pupils by year of birth.

items.paragraph: Schools sort children by year of birth so routinely that the practice seems like a law of nature rather than an administrative convenience. Yet grouping by age assumes that children born within the same twelve months are ready for the same material at the same moment, an assumption that every experienced teacher knows to be false. In classrooms that deliberately mix ages, the older children consolidate what they know by explaining it, and the younger ones see, in the work of those just ahead of them, what the next step looks like. None of this makes mixed-age teaching easy: it demands careful planning and a teacher able to manage several levels at once, and without these it can fail badly. But that difficulty is a reason to prepare teachers for the task, not a reason to treat the age-graded class as the only sensible arrangement.
